day.day_focus: Luke 15:29-30 - Many years I have been serving you and I have never neglected a command of yours

scripture.text: But he answered and said to his father, ‘Look! For so many years I have been serving you and I have never neglected a command of yours; and yet you have never given me a young goat, so that I might celebrate with my friends; but when this son of yours came, who has devoured your wealth with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’

exposition.text: Luke 15:29-30 opens with a scene marked by self-righteous resentment that refuses the joy of grace. The text does not ask the reader to admire the moment from a distance. The passage puts one clear scene in front of us: Many years I have been serving the hearer and I have never neglected a command of yours. We should stay with that scene before we rush to a slogan. What the passage shows through many, years, been must be received before it is applied. That keeps the reading honest. religious pride can remain near the father's house while hating the father's mercy and joy. Luke 15:29-30 stays concrete through He answered and said to his father — the specific language of many, years, been does the work before any principle is named. What Luke 15:29-30 puts before the reader is not abstract: many years i have been serving the hearer and i have never neglected a command of yours. The text does not explain the scene from a distance — it names what people do when Jesus is near. The point is not bare information. It presses into faithful response instead of vague admiration. We should not drift into generic encouragement detached from the scene. We should let the passage name the pressure point for the day. If the scene is shaped by Many years I have been serving the hearer and I have never neglected a command of yours, then obedience today should answer that same pressure point. Where the text exposes fear, we should answer the word with concrete obedience. Where it honors devotion, we should practice repentance from resentful self-righteousness that measures grace like wages instead of receiving it as family mercy. Where it reveals Jesus clearly, we should pursue steady trust in the ordinary places of life rather than delay. That keeps the day under the authority of Scripture. Strong exposition stays close to the text. It does not chase a clever slogan. It lets the details do their work on the conscience. That kind of reading slows us down. It teaches us to listen before we react. It also keeps prayer and application from drifting away from the passage. The passage sustains courage because Jesus remains worthy of trust in costly moments. The church's witness is strengthened when daily conduct aligns with confessed doctrine. The text rewards slow attention because its details are part of its theology, not background decoration. Good application therefore grows from disciplined reading rather than from devotional instinct alone. prompts: Sit with Luke 15:29-30 for two quiet minutes. Read the scene of self-righteous resentment that refuses the joy of grace slowly and let it settle before you move on.
Where does this passage call for repentance from resentful self-righteousness that measures grace like wages instead of receiving it as family mercy today?
Stay for one more minute and answer God with one honest sentence of trust, repentance, or gratitude before continuing.

items: Before your next decision, pause and ask how Luke 15:29-30 should shape your response.
Offer one concrete act of service that matches the patience or steadiness this passage commends.
action_steps.connector_phrase: Because Luke 15:29-30 calls for repentance from resentful self-righteousness that measures grace like wages instead of receiving it as family mercy today:

prayer.text: Father, thank You for speaking clearly in Luke 15:29-30. In this passage You bring self-righteous resentment that refuses the joy of grace into the open through Many years I have been serving the hearer and I have never neglected a command of yours. Lord Jesus, keep us from reading these words as distant history only, and press them into our ordinary obedience today. Where we resist the truth highlighted in this reflection, bring repentance and renewed trust. Keep us near Your word, and do not let ordinary pressure turn us away from humble obedience. Holy Spirit, take what we have seen in the exposition and turn it into worship instead of mere information. Teach us to remember that Luke 15:29-30 opens with a scene marked by self-righteous resentment that refuses the joy of grace. Guard our speech from haste, our work from pride, and our choices from whatever would pull us away from faithful response instead of vague admiration. Amen.
